Reference: Ryan (2012)

Model Setting

The paper measures the product-market welfare cost of the 1990 Amendments to the Clean Air Act in the US Portland cement industry. The usual regulatory cost analysis is an engineering estimate of compliance expenditures. In a concentrated industry where sunk entry costs and lumpy capacity investment determine market structure, such a static analysis misses the effect of regulation on entry, investment and market power. The paper builds a dynamic oligopoly model in the tradition of Ericson and Pakes (1995): in each regional market, firms that differ only in capacity play a capacity-constrained Cournot game every year and make entry, exit and capacity adjustment decisions subject to private cost shocks. The whole cost structure is estimated with the two-step estimator of Bajari, Benkard and Levin (2007), hereafter BBL, separately for the years before and after 1990, and the Markov-perfect equilibrium is then computed under the two estimated distributions of sunk entry costs.

The main finding is that the Amendments left production costs and investment costs essentially unchanged but raised the mean sunk cost of entry by 22 percent, from about 183 to about 223 million dollars. Lower entry leads to fewer and larger firms, slightly higher prices and lower output. Product-market surplus falls by between 810 million and 3.2 billion dollars in present value (the introduction of the paper says 820 million for the lower bound). In a mature market consumers lose, potential entrants lose, and incumbents gain from softer competition, so a static analysis that counts only the compliance cost of incumbents obtains the wrong sign for their welfare change and understates the total cost by at least 300 million dollars. The benefits of cleaner air are not measured.

Industry and Regulation

Portland cement is the binding ingredient of concrete. It is a homogeneous good (producers follow a common technical specification), it cannot be stored for long, and it is costly to transport relative to its value: reported transport costs rise from 5.79 dollars per ton within 50 miles to 25.85 dollars per ton beyond 500 miles, and 82.5 percent of cement is shipped less than 200 miles. Competition is therefore local, and the paper takes the regional markets defined by the US Geological Survey as independent markets. In 2000 the industry had 116 plants operated by about 40 firms and produced 86 million tons worth about 8.7 billion dollars; the median market has four firms. Production takes place in enormous rotary kilns, so capacity is added in lumps and most firms do not change capacity in most years. Imports are treated as a permanent shifter of the demand for domestic cement.

The 1990 Amendments defined new categories of regulated pollutants (hazardous air pollutants and volatile organic compounds), but the Environmental Protection Agency did not issue final emission requirements for them for 12 years, so there was no direct change in variable costs during the sample. Two components bound immediately. Under Title V, every plant emitting significant quantities had to obtain an operating permit, install monitoring equipment, write compliance plans and undergo certification testing; industry estimates put this at 5 to 10 million dollars per plant and the agency at no more than 5 million dollars. In addition, brand new plants had to pass a further rigorous environmental certification, with engineering reports on local air and water quality, which industry sources put at another 5 to 10 million dollars for a greenfield facility. The New Source Review permits created by the 1977 Amendments also burden new and substantially modified plants, but they did not change during the sample and are not modeled separately. Because the new certification applies to entrants and the emission standards were not yet in force, the natural place for the Amendments to show up is the sunk cost of entry. The data cover 1980 to 1999: prices and quantities for 27 regional markets (517 market-year observations) from the Minerals Yearbook, and plant capacities and production from the Portland Cement Association (an unbalanced panel of 2233 plant-year observations for 1980 to 1998).

Timing, State and Product Market

A market is described by the Nˉ×1\bar{N}\times1Nˉ×1 state vector sts_tst​, where sits_{it}sit​ is the capacity of firm iii in year ttt and Nˉ\bar{N}Nˉ is an exogenous maximal number of active firms. A firm with zero capacity is a potential entrant. Time is discrete and infinite, a period is one year, and the discount factor is fixed at β=0.9\beta=0.9β=0.9. Within a period: (i) each incumbent privately draws a scrap value and decides whether to exit; (ii) potential entrants privately draw entry and investment costs, continuing incumbents privately draw fixed costs of investment and divestment, and all firms simultaneously choose entry and capacity adjustment; (iii) incumbents, including those that have decided to exit, compete in quantities; (iv) entry, exit and capacity changes are realized. Transitions are deterministic and take one period, and there is no depreciation. Each firm acts independently across markets. In market mmm demand has constant elasticity:

Adjustment, Entry and Exit Costs

A firm changes its capacity by xix_ixi​ at cost:

An entrant pays both the sunk entry cost and the cost of its initial capacity, earns nothing in the entry period, and becomes an incumbent next period. It enters only when the sum of its two draws κi+γ1i\kappa_i+\gamma_{1i}κi​+γ1i​ is low enough. A Markov-perfect Nash equilibrium (MPNE) is a strategy profile such that no firm gains from a unilateral deviation:

Vi(s;σi∗(s),σ−i(s),θ,εi)≥Vi(s;σ~i(s),σ−i(s),θ,εi)(10)V_i(s;\sigma^*_i(s),\sigma_{-i}(s),\theta,\varepsilon_i)\geq V_i(s;\tilde{\sigma}_i(s),\sigma_{-i}(s),\theta,\varepsilon_i) \tag{10}Vi​(s;σi∗​(s),σ−i​(s),θ,εi​)≥Vi​(s;σ~i​(s),σ−i​(s),θ,εi​)(10)

for all sss, all εi\varepsilon_iεi​ and all alternative strategies σ~i(s)\tilde{\sigma}_i(s)σ~i​(s); the same inequality holds after integrating out εi\varepsilon_iεi​. Private information on the discrete actions makes best responses continuous, so a pure-strategy equilibrium exists (Doraszelski and Satterthwaite 2010), but it need not be unique. Two assumptions deal with this in estimation: the same equilibrium is played in all markets, so that policy functions can be estimated by pooling markets, and firms treat the regulatory environment as permanent, so that the Amendments are an unanticipated one-time change (as in Rothwell and Rust 1995).

Step One: Demand and Production Costs

Demand and production are static, so their parameters are estimated directly, before and independently of the dynamic parameters. The estimated demand equation for market jjj in year ttt is:

ln⁡Qjt=α0+α1ln⁡Pjt+α2j+α3t′Xjt+εjt(11)\ln Q_{jt}=\alpha_0+\alpha_1\ln P_{jt}+\alpha_{2j}+\alpha'_{3t}X_{jt}+\varepsilon_{jt} \tag{11}lnQjt​=α0​+α1​lnPjt​+α2j​+α3t′​Xjt​+εjt​(11)

where α2j\alpha_{2j}α2j​ is a market demand shifter, XjtX_{jt}Xjt​ collects covariates (log population, log housing permits, time trends, depending on the specification) and εjt\varepsilon_{jt}εjt​ is an i.i.d. demand shock. Price is instrumented with supply-side cost shifters: coal prices, natural gas prices, electricity rates and skilled manufacturing wages. The preferred specification has market fixed effects and no other covariates. Production costs are estimated by nonlinear least squares: for each guess of δ\deltaδ the capacity-constrained Cournot quantities are computed for every firm in every market and year (the fixed point is easy to find because best responses slope downward), and δ\deltaδ is chosen to minimize the sum of squared differences between observed and predicted quantities. The fixed cost is not identified, because every firm produces in every period, and the paper assumes δ0=0\delta_0=0δ0​=0. The threshold is kept inside the unit interval by estimating ν~\tilde{\nu}ν~ in:

ν=exp⁡(ν~)1.0+exp⁡(ν~)(12)\nu=\frac{\exp(\tilde{\nu})}{1.0+\exp(\tilde{\nu})} \tag{12}ν=1.0+exp(ν~)exp(ν~)​(12)

Each of δ1\delta_1δ1​, δ2\delta_2δ2​ and ν~\tilde{\nu}ν~ has a post-1990 dummy shifter, which is how a change in production costs after the Amendments is tested. A firm with several plants in one market is treated as one plant with the summed capacity. The annual capacity reported in the plant data is interpreted as the quantity actually produced, and the daily boilerplate rating as capacity.

For capacity adjustment the paper uses an (S,s)(S,s)(S,s) rule, following the empirical model of Attanasio (2000), because fixed adjustment costs make firms tolerate deviations from their desired capacity. A firm has a target capacity sit∗s^*_{it}sit∗​ to which it moves whenever it adjusts:

The paper prints the band equations with the sum of competitors' quantities qjtq_{jt}qjt​; this is a misprint, corrected here to capacities as in the target equation, the text and the result tables. The band errors u‾itb\underline{u}^b_{it}u​itb​ and uˉitb\bar{u}^b_{it}uˉitb​ are i.i.d. normal with mean zero and equal variance and are independent of uit∗u^*_{it}uit∗​. Step Two: Minimum Distance

The second stage finds the dynamic parameters that make the estimated policies optimal. Integrating the private shocks out of the per-period payoff gives:

Eεiπi(s,σ(s);θ)=  πˉi(s)⋅1−pi(s)⋅(γ~1i+γ2xi+γ3xi2)−pd(s)⋅(γ~4i+γ5xi+γ6xi2)+pe(s)⋅ϕ~i(17)\begin{aligned} E_{\varepsilon_i}\pi_i(s,\sigma(s);\theta)=\;&\bar{\pi}_i(s)\cdot1-p_i(s)\cdot\left(\widetilde{\gamma}_{1i}+\gamma_2x_i+\gamma_3x_i^2\right)\\ &-p_d(s)\cdot\left(\widetilde{\gamma}_{4i}+\gamma_5x_i+\gamma_6x_i^2\right)+p_e(s)\cdot\widetilde{\phi}_i \end{aligned} \tag{17}Eεi​​πi​(s,σ(s);θ)=​πˉi​(s)⋅1−pi​(s)⋅(γ​1i​+γ2​xi​+γ3​xi2​)−pd​(s)⋅(γ​4i​+γ5​xi​+γ6​xi2​)+pe​(s)⋅ϕ​i​​(17)

with a tensor product of linear b-splines on the unit square, and symmetrically for γ~4i\widetilde{\gamma}_{4i}γ​4i​. In practice each conditional mean is made a function of its own action's probability only, because under the estimated (S,s)(S,s)(S,s) rule no state has a positive probability of both investment and divestment. This is the device that recovers distributions rather than only means: the estimated spline traces out the truncated mean of the draw at each choice probability, which pins down the underlying distribution (the argument is in the paper's supplement), and the reported means and standard deviations are the projection of the spline coefficients onto normal distributions. where the product-market profit is known from the first step and is multiplied by 1, and ζ\zetaζ stacks the remaining terms of the expected payoff (action probabilities, adjustment sizes and spline bases; the paper does not list its elements). Sunk Entry Costs and Standard Errors

Entry costs are recovered last, since the entry decision of a short-lived entrant is a static comparison once the value of being an incumbent is known. The paper restates the entrant's value as:

Vie(s;σ(s),θ,εi)=max⁡{0,max⁡xi≥0[−κi−γ1i−γ2xi−γ3xi2+βE(V(s′)∣s,σ(s))]}(26)V^e_i(s;\sigma(s),\theta,\varepsilon_i)=\max\left\{0,\max_{x_i\geq0}\left[-\kappa_i-\gamma_{1i}-\gamma_2x_i-\gamma_3x_i^2+\beta E(V(s')\mid s,\sigma(s))\right]\right\} \tag{26}Vie​(s;σ(s),θ,εi​)=max{0,xi​≥0max​[−κi​−γ1i​−γ2​xi​−γ3​xi2​+βE(V(s′)∣s,σ(s))]}(26)

Everything here is known or computable except the distribution of κi\kappa_iκi​, which is assumed normal with mean μκ\mu_\kappaμκ​ and variance σκ2\sigma^2_\kappaσκ2​. Writing EVe(s)EV^e(s)EVe(s) for the expected value of entering at state sss gross of the two fixed-cost draws, the firm enters when their sum is below this value, and the sum of two independent normals is normal:

Pr⁡(κi+γ1i≤EVe(s))=Φ(EVe(s);μκ+μγ+,σκ2+σγ+2)(27)\Pr\left(\kappa_i+\gamma_{1i}\leq EV^e(s)\right)=\Phi\left(EV^e(s);\mu_\kappa+\mu^+_\gamma,\sigma^2_\kappa+\sigma^{+2}_\gamma\right) \tag{27}Pr(κi​+γ1i​≤EVe(s))=Φ(EVe(s);μκ​+μγ+​,σκ2​+σγ+2​)(27)

The left-hand side is the entry probit of the first step and EVe(s)EV^e(s)EVe(s) is obtained by forward simulation. For NSNSNS states sis_isi​ the parameters solve:

min⁡{μκ,σκ2}1NS∑i=1NS[Pr⁡(entry∣si)−Φ(EVe(si);μκ+μγ+,σκ2+σγ+2)]2(28)\min_{\{\mu_\kappa,\sigma^2_\kappa\}}\frac{1}{NS}\sum_{i=1}^{NS}\left[\Pr(\text{entry}\mid s_i)-\Phi\left(EV^e(s_i);\mu_\kappa+\mu^+_\gamma,\sigma^2_\kappa+\sigma^{+2}_\gamma\right)\right]^2 \tag{28}{μκ​,σκ2​}min​NS1​i=1∑NS​[Pr(entry∣si​)−Φ(EVe(si​);μκ​+μγ+​,σκ2​+σγ+2​)]2(28)

The states vary incumbent capacity from 500 thousand to 3 million tons per year in steps of 5 thousand tons, with 250 simulation replications per state. The mean is identified by the level of the entry probability and the variance by how fast that probability moves with the value of entry across states. The problem is solved separately for the years before and after 1990, using the post-1990 dummy in the entry probit and the period-specific value functions. To summarize how parameters may change in 1990: production costs have dummy shifters, the investment policy and all dynamic parameters are estimated separately by period, and the entry and exit probits have a post-1990 dummy. Standard errors of the dynamic parameters and of the counterfactual outcomes come from subsampling without replacement at the level of market histories (Politis and Romano 1994): 500 subsamples of 19 complete market histories.

Key Estimates

  • Demand: the preferred specification (market fixed effects) gives α1=−2.96\alpha_1=-2.96α1​=−2.96 with standard error 0.378; without covariates the elasticity is −3.21-3.21−3.21, and with market time trends it is −2.26-2.26−2.26. The first-stage F-statistic is 42.99. Specifications with both population and market fixed effects give small, insignificant elasticities and are rejected because they would imply investment costs of several billion dollars per plant.

  • Production costs: δ1=31.58\delta_1=31.58δ1​=31.58 dollars per ton (standard error 1.91), δ2=1.239\delta_2=1.239δ2​=1.239 and ν~=1.916\tilde{\nu}=1.916ν~=1.916, so the penalty starts at about 87 percent utilisation and few plants exceed 90 percent. The three post-1990 shifters (2.41, −0.0299-0.0299−0.0299 and 0.0917) are statistically insignificant, so the Amendments did not change marginal costs. The implied average price is 57.81 dollars per ton, average annual revenue about 39 million dollars and profit 16.5 million dollars, a margin of 39 percent.

  • Policy functions: the target regression has an adjusted R-squared of 0.9994 and the band regression 0.8952. In the exit probit the post-1990 dummy is −0.595-0.595−0.595 and lowers the exit probability at the mean from 2.1 to 0.4 percent (51 exits before 1990 and 6 after); in the entry probit it is −0.609-0.609−0.609 (15 entries before and 4 after).

  • Investment costs: the marginal cost of new capacity is 230 dollars per ton before 1990 and 238 after (standard errors 85 and 51), close to accounting estimates of about 200 dollars per ton, so a plant of 1.5 million tons costs about 350 million dollars. The quadratic term γ3\gamma_3γ3​ is set to zero. The mean fixed cost of investment μγ+\mu^+_\gammaμγ+​ is 0.62 million dollars before and 1.25 million after, an insignificant difference. Divestment is prohibitively costly, with a mean fixed cost μγ−\mu^-_\gammaμγ−​ of about 298 million dollars before and 307 million after.

  • Scrap values: the mean is −62.6-62.6−62.6 million dollars before 1990 and −53.3-53.3−53.3 million after, with standard deviations of 75.6 and 69.8 million. Exit therefore needs a very favorable draw: the probability of a draw above 75 million dollars is 3.4 percent before and 3.3 percent after.

  • Sunk entry costs: μκ\mu_\kappaμκ​ rises from 182.6 million dollars (standard error 36.9) to 223.3 million (45.9), an increase of 22 percent that is statistically significant (the subsampled mean difference is 43.7 million with standard error 21.2), while σκ\sigma_\kappaσκ​ moves from 101.9 to 97.4 million. The probability of a draw below 10 million dollars falls from 4.5 to 1.4 percent, and below 50 million dollars from 9.6 to 3.8 percent. This increase is far larger than the 5 to 10 million dollars of direct certification costs quoted by industry sources.

Counterfactuals

The policy experiment solves the MPNE of the model twice: once with the full post-1990 cost structure, and once with the post-1990 cost structure but the pre-1990 distribution of sunk entry costs, so the difference isolates the entry-cost channel. The equilibrium is computed by iterating on the value and policy functions, which are approximated with b-spline interpolation as in Fowlie, Reguant and Ryan (2010), until the change in their norm is below 10−810^{-8}10−8; uniqueness is not guaranteed, so the paper documents the algorithm. For computational reasons the market has at most four firms (the median market size), demand is that of Alabama, and demand does not grow. Each equilibrium is simulated along 25,000 paths of 200 periods from two starting states. All amounts are present values, with subsampled standard errors of the differences in parentheses.

  • De novo market (no incumbents, four potential entrants; an upper bound): total welfare falls by about 120 million dollars (49), a little over 5 percent. Periods with four active firms fall from 135.9 to 84.0 and periods with three firms rise from 54.7 to 91.4. The average active firm is about 7 percent larger, the price rises from 66.66 to 68.12 dollars per ton and quantity falls by 3.4 percent. Consumer surplus falls by 66 million dollars (58), or 3.4 percent, which is 55 percent of the total loss. Producer profit falls from 43.9 to about 33.4 million dollars: entrants pay more and also enter at higher cost draws because they expect fewer rivals, so the prospective oligopoly rents are competed away.

  • Mature market (incumbents of 0.75 and 1.5 million tons, two potential entrants; a lower bound): total welfare falls by 30 million dollars (18), slightly less than 1 percent. Periods with four firms fall by 40 percent, the price rises by 1.44 dollars and quantity falls by 3.3 percent. Consumer surplus falls by about 63 million dollars (33), or 2.8 percent, while total producer profit rises by 9.5 million dollars (5.5), or 4.2 percent, and the profit of the largest incumbent rises by 32.9 million dollars (19.1), or 6 percent.

  • Aggregate cost: summing the per-market losses over all 27 markets gives a lower bound of over 810 million dollars (486) and an upper bound of 3.2 billion dollars (1.3 billion); the upper bound corresponds to restarting the whole industry from scratch.

  • Static versus dynamic analysis: an engineering analysis would charge each incumbent its Title V compliance cost and stop there. In the dynamic equilibrium the large incumbent is better off under the Amendments as long as its permit costs less than 32.9 million dollars, because higher entry costs shield it from competition. The static analysis therefore gets the sign wrong for incumbents, ignores the loss to consumers and the distributional shift from potential entrants to incumbents, and with a certification cost of at most 5 million dollars per installation understates the welfare cost by at least 300 million dollars. Lower output also lowers emissions, which is not valued here.

This is the assumed demand curve of regional market mmm: the log of aggregate quantity QmQ_mQm​ is linear in the log of price PmP_mPm​. Quantities are in thousands of tons per year and prices in dollars per ton.

The constant-elasticity form is chosen because it is estimated by a linear instrumental-variables regression, equation (11), and because it gives a simple inverse demand for the quantity game:

The indicator 1(qi>νsi)1(q_i>\nu s_i)1(qi​>νsi​) switches the penalty on. Marginal cost is therefore:

∂Ci∂qi=δ1+2δ21(qi>νsi)(qi−νsi)\frac{\partial C_i}{\partial q_i}=\delta_1+2\delta_21(q_i>\nu s_i)(q_i-\nu s_i)∂qi​∂Ci​​=δ1​+2δ2​1(qi​>νsi​)(qi​−νsi​)

The paper says that costs increase as the square of the percentage of capacity utilisation, which would suggest a penalty in qi/si−νq_i/s_i-\nuqi​/si​−ν. The printed formula is in the level qi−νsiq_i-\nu s_iqi​−νsi​, and the level form is the one that agrees with the rest of the paper: the results section speaks of linearly increasing marginal costs, and the magnitudes above only make sense in levels. Capacity sis_isi​ enters profits only through this function, which is what makes it the payoff-relevant state in equations (3) and (4).

This equation is written by the author of the note; the paper only names the product-market profit πˉi(s;α,δ)\bar{\pi}_i(s;\alpha,\delta)πˉi​(s;α,δ) and says that firms play a capacity-constrained Cournot game. It defines that profit: revenue at the market price Pm(Qm)P_m(Q_m)Pm​(Qm​), read off the inverse of the demand curve (1) at total output Qm=∑jqjQ_m=\sum_jq_jQm​=∑j​qj​, minus the production cost (2).

Three points of interpretation. First, the right-hand side is evaluated at the Nash equilibrium quantities of the one-shot game, that is, the quantities that solve the first-order condition (4) for all active firms simultaneously. Since demand and cost parameters are fixed and the only firm-specific variable in the cost function is capacity, those quantities, and hence the profit, are functions of the capacity vector sss alone. That is why the left-hand side has sss as its only argument. Second, the capacity constraint is the soft one built into CiC_iCi​: there is no separate restriction qi≤siq_i\leq s_iqi​≤si​. Third, there are no dynamic terms here. Output is not storable and does not affect future states, so the quantity game is static and can be solved separately from the investment problem.

This separation is what the estimation exploits. Demand (11) and production costs are estimated first, πˉi(s)\bar{\pi}_i(s)πˉi​(s) is then a known function, and it enters the dynamic payoff (7) and the linear representation (21) with a known coefficient of one. With δ0=0\delta_0=0δ0​=0 the profit is positive for every active firm: at the estimates the average firm earns revenue of about 39 million dollars and profit of about 16.5 million dollars a year.

This first-order condition is also the note author's; it is derived here from equations (1), (2) and (3). Firm iii chooses qiq_iqi​ to maximize profit (3), taking the outputs of its rivals as given, so that ∂Qm/∂qi=1\partial Q_m/\partial q_i=1∂Qm​/∂qi​=1:

The fixed costs γ1i\gamma_{1i}γ1i​ and γ4i\gamma_{4i}γ4i​ are the stochastic elements: they are private draws, new every period, from normal distributions with means μγ+,μγ−\mu^+_\gamma,\mu^-_\gammaμγ+​,μγ−​ and standard deviations σγ+,σγ−\sigma^+_\gamma,\sigma^-_\gammaσγ+​,σγ−​. On signs: Γ\GammaΓ is a cost and is subtracted in the payoff (7). This function collects the two lump-sum payments that are tied to changes in a firm's status and not to production or to the size of an investment. It enters the per-period payoff (7) with a plus sign, so the signs inside the cases are payoff signs: a new entrant pays the sunk entry cost, hence −κi-\kappa_i−κi​, and an exiting firm receives its scrap value, hence +ϕi+\phi_i+ϕi​. The printed definition lists only these two cases; for an incumbent that continues, and for a potential entrant that stays out, the value is zero.

Both objects are private draws. The entry cost κi\kappa_iκi​ comes from the common distribution FκF_\kappaFκ​ and is drawn once, by the single short-lived potential entrant of the period. The scrap value ϕi\phi_iϕi​ comes from FϕF_\phiFϕ​ and is drawn anew by every incumbent in every period; it can be negative when clean-up costs exceed the proceeds from selling the site. Independence across firms, over time and from the adjustment-cost draws of equation (5) is what later allows each draw to be integrated out separately.

The function is where the paper's main result lives. The exit branch gives the stopping rule in the incumbent's value function (8) and the exit probability (18), from which the distribution of ϕi\phi_iϕi​ is recovered through equation (19). The entry branch gives the entrant's problem (9) and (26), from which the distribution of κi\kappa_iκi​ is recovered through equations (27) and (28). The estimated mean of κi\kappa_iκi​ rises from 182.6 to 223.3 million dollars after 1990, while the mean scrap value is negative in both periods (−62.6-62.6−62.6 and −53.3-53.3−53.3 million dollars), so exit occurs only at draws from the far right tail.

The per-period payoff adds up everything a firm receives or pays in one year: the Cournot profit πˉi\bar{\pi}_iπˉi​ of equation (3), minus the adjustment cost Γ\GammaΓ of equation (5), plus the entry or exit payment Φi\Phi_iΦi​ of equation (6). The arguments record what each piece depends on: the state sss and the demand and cost parameters for the product market, the firm's own adjustment xix_ixi​ (a component of its action aia_iai​) and its draws γi=(γ1i,γ4i)\gamma_i=(\gamma_{1i},\gamma_{4i})γi​=(γ1i​,γ4i​) for adjustment, and the status change together with κi\kappa_iκi​ or ϕi\phi_iϕi​ for the last term.

By type of firm and action the payoff is:

An exiting incumbent still produces in its last period, and an entrant pays for its plant one period before it can produce, because capacity changes take one period.

The payoff is additively separable and linear in the unknown dynamic parameters (the γ\gammaγ coefficients and the draws), with the product-market term known from the first step. This is what the second step relies on: taking expectations over the private draws gives equation (17), which is linear in parameters as in equation (21), and discounting and summing gives the value function (23). The parameters of this function are what the note calls θ\thetaθ.

The value function follows from the within-period timing by backward induction. Let Ui(x)U_i(x)Ui​(x) denote the discounted expected continuation value when the firm's own capacity moves to si+xs_i+xsi​+x and rivals follow σ\sigmaσ:

Ui(x)=β∫EεiVi(s′;σ(s′),θ,εi) dP(si+x,s−i′;s,σ(s))U_i(x)=\beta\int E_{\varepsilon_i}V_i(s';\sigma(s'),\theta,\varepsilon_i)\,dP(s_i+x,s'_{-i};s,\sigma(s))Ui​(x)=β∫Eεi​​Vi​(s′;σ(s′),θ,εi​)dP(si​+x,s−i′​;s,σ(s))

The inner expectation is over next period's private draws; the integral is over rivals' next-period capacities, which are random from the firm's point of view because rivals' entry, exit and investment depend on their private draws. The firm's own transition is deterministic.

Last stage: a firm that has decided to stay observes γ1i\gamma_{1i}γ1i​ and γ4i\gamma_{4i}γ4i​ and chooses among investing, divesting and doing nothing. Using the cost function (5), the three options are worth:

Vi+(s)−γ1i=max⁡x>0[−γ2x−γ3x2+Ui(x)]−γ1iVi−(s)−γ4i=max⁡x<0[−γ5x−γ6x2+Ui(x)]−γ4iVi0(s)=Ui(0)\begin{aligned} V^+_i(s)-\gamma_{1i}&=\max_{x>0}\left[-\gamma_2x-\gamma_3x^2+U_i(x)\right]-\gamma_{1i}\\ V^-_i(s)-\gamma_{4i}&=\max_{x<0}\left[-\gamma_5x-\gamma_6x^2+U_i(x)\right]-\gamma_{4i}\\ V^0_i(s)&=U_i(0) \end{aligned}Vi+​(s)−γ1i​Vi−​(s)−γ4i​Vi0​(s)​=x>0max​[−γ2​x−γ3​x2+Ui​(x)]−γ1i​=x<0max​[−γ5​x−γ6​x2+Ui​(x)]−γ4i​=Ui​(0)​

The fixed costs do not depend on xxx, so they do not affect the optimal size of an adjustment, only whether one is made.

First stage: the firm knows ϕi\phi_iϕi​ but not yet the adjustment draws. Exiting yields ϕi\phi_iϕi​; staying yields the expectation of the best of the three options. Product-market profit is earned either way, since exiting firms produce in their last period. Hence:

Vi(s;σ(s),θ,εi)=πˉi(s;θ)+max⁡{ϕi,  Eεimax⁡[Vi+(s)−γ1i,  Vi−(s)−γ4i,  Vi0(s)]}V_i(s;\sigma(s),\theta,\varepsilon_i)=\bar{\pi}_i(s;\theta)+\max\left\{\phi_i,\;E_{\varepsilon_i}\max\left[V^+_i(s)-\gamma_{1i},\;V^-_i(s)-\gamma_{4i},\;V^0_i(s)\right]\right\}Vi​(s;σ(s),θ,εi​)=πˉi​(s;θ)+max{ϕi​,Eεi​​max[Vi+​(s)−γ1i​,Vi−​(s)−γ4i​,Vi0​(s)]}

Vie=max⁡{0,  EVe(s)−κi−γ1i},enter if and only if κi+γ1i≤EVe(s)V^e_i=\max\left\{0,\;EV^e(s)-\kappa_i-\gamma_{1i}\right\},\qquad\text{enter if and only if }\kappa_i+\gamma_{1i}\leq EV^e(s)Vie​=max{0,EVe(s)−κi​−γ1i​},enter if and only if κi​+γ1i​≤EVe(s)

This is the statement that a firm enters only when the sum of its two draws is low enough, and it is the basis of equation (27). The strict inequality x>0x>0x>0 matters: it rules out paying κi\kappa_iκi​ to hold an empty slot and waiting for a good investment draw. Because the outside option is zero and there is no waiting, the entry decision is a static threshold rule once ViV_iVi​ is known.

This is the equilibrium requirement. The left-hand side is the value to firm iii at state sss and private draws εi\varepsilon_iεi​ when it follows the strategy σi∗\sigma^*_iσi∗​ and its rivals follow σ−i\sigma_{-i}σ−i​; the right-hand side is its value under any other strategy σ~i\tilde{\sigma}_iσ~i​ with rivals' strategies unchanged. A profile is a Markov-perfect Nash equilibrium when the inequality holds for every firm, every state, every realization of the draws and every alternative. Strategies are Markovian (they depend on the history only through the current sss and εi\varepsilon_iεi​), symmetric and anonymous (firms with the same capacity and draws act alike), so one set of policy functions describes all firms and σ−i\sigma_{-i}σ−i​ is the same function applied to the rivals.

Because the inequality holds draw by draw, it also holds on average:

EεiVi(s;σi∗(s),σ−i(s),θ,εi)≥EεiVi(s;σ~i(s),σ−i(s),θ,εi)E_{\varepsilon_i}V_i(s;\sigma^*_i(s),\sigma_{-i}(s),\theta,\varepsilon_i)\geq E_{\varepsilon_i}V_i(s;\tilde{\sigma}_i(s),\sigma_{-i}(s),\theta,\varepsilon_i)Eεi​​Vi​(s;σi∗​(s),σ−i​(s),θ,εi​)≥Eεi​​Vi​(s;σ~i​(s),σ−i​(s),θ,εi​)

This ex ante version is the one used in estimation, since the econometrician does not observe εi\varepsilon_iεi​.

The condition has no free parameters to fit by itself; its role is to turn observed behaviour into restrictions on θ\thetaθ. If the policies estimated in the first step are the equilibrium policies, then at the true θ\thetaθ no perturbation of firm iii's policy can raise its value. Equation (23) writes each side as a linear function of θ\thetaθ, equation (24) takes the difference, and equation (25) chooses θ\thetaθ to make violations as small as possible. The inequality is necessary for equilibrium but there may be several equilibria, which is why the paper assumes that the same one is played in all markets.

This is the estimating version of the demand curve (1). The unit of observation is regional market jjj in year ttt (517 observations, 27 markets). The dependent variable is log quantity, α1\alpha_1α1​ is the elasticity, α2j\alpha_{2j}α2j​ is a market fixed effect, XjtX_{jt}Xjt​ holds optional shifters (log population, log housing permits, trends) with coefficient vector α3t\alpha_{3t}α3t​, and εjt\varepsilon_{jt}εjt​ is an i.i.d. demand shock. In the preferred specification there are only market fixed effects, so the intercept of equation (1) corresponds to:

α0m=α0+α2jfor market m=j\alpha_{0m}=\alpha_0+\alpha_{2j}\quad\text{for market }m=jα0m​=α0​+α2j​for market m=j

Price is endogenous: a high demand shock raises both quantity and the Cournot price, which biases the least squares coefficient toward zero. The instruments are cost shifters that move the supply relation (4) but are excluded from demand: coal and natural gas prices, electricity rates and skilled manufacturing wages. Cement production is energy intensive, so they are relevant (first-stage F of 42.99); the exclusion restriction is that local energy prices and wages do not move construction demand directly. With market fixed effects, α1\alpha_1α1​ is identified from within-market co-movement of quantity with the part of price explained by input costs.

The estimate matters twice later. It sets the markup in the first-order condition (4), since the Lerner index is the market share divided by ∣α1∣|\alpha_1|∣α1​∣, and it scales all dynamic cost estimates, because investment and entry costs are inferred from the profits firms forgo. The paper chooses α1=−2.96\alpha_1=-2.96α1​=−2.96 partly because low-elasticity specifications imply implausibly large investment costs.

This is a reparameterisation, not a behavioural assumption. The threshold ν\nuν of the cost function (2) is a share of capacity and must lie between zero and one. The nonlinear least squares routine searches over an unrestricted real number ν~\tilde{\nu}ν~ and maps it into the unit interval with the logistic function; the constant printed as 1.0 is simply one. The map is strictly increasing with inverse:

ν~=ln⁡ν1−ν\tilde{\nu}=\ln\frac{\nu}{1-\nu}ν~=ln1−νν​

so nothing is lost and no boundary constraint has to be imposed on the optimizer. At the estimate ν~=1.916\tilde{\nu}=1.916ν~=1.916:

ν=exp⁡(1.916)1+exp⁡(1.916)=6.7947.794≈0.872\nu=\frac{\exp(1.916)}{1+\exp(1.916)}=\frac{6.794}{7.794}\approx0.872ν=1+exp(1.916)exp(1.916)​=7.7946.794​≈0.872

which is the statement that the penalty starts at about 87 percent utilisation. With the post-1990 shifter of 0.0917 added, ν~=2.008\tilde{\nu}=2.008ν~=2.008 and ν≈0.882\nu\approx0.882ν≈0.882, a change of one percentage point that is not statistically significant.

Standard errors reported for ν~\tilde{\nu}ν~ translate to ν\nuν by the delta method, using the derivative of the logistic function:

dνdν~=ν(1−ν)≈0.112\frac{d\nu}{d\tilde{\nu}}=\nu(1-\nu)\approx0.112dν~dν​=ν(1−ν)≈0.112

so the reported standard error of 0.010 on ν~\tilde{\nu}ν~ corresponds to roughly 0.001 on ν\nuν. The threshold is identified by the ratio of output to capacity at which firms bunch: equation (4) shows that output sits just above νsi\nu s_iνsi​, and the estimate is close to the coefficient of about 0.86 in the paper's regression of output on capacity.

This is the first half of the investment policy function, the reduced-form description of what firms do that the two-step method needs. The target sit∗s^*_{it}sit∗​ is the capacity a firm moves to if it adjusts at all. Its log is a flexible function of the two state variables that matter to firm iii under symmetry and anonymity: its own capacity sits_{it}sit​ and the total capacity of its rivals ∑j≠isjt\sum_{j\neq i}s_{jt}∑j=i​sjt​. The function bs(⋅)\text{bs}(\cdot)bs(⋅) is a vector of cubic b-spline basis functions, piecewise polynomials on a grid of knots, so λ1′bs(sit)\lambda'_1\text{bs}(s_{it})λ1′​bs(sit​) is a smooth curve whose shape is left to the data; this is a linear sieve, estimated by least squares. The error uit∗u^*_{it}uit∗​ has mean zero and captures everything else that moves the target.

The specification is additive in the two variables (no interactions) and summarizes rivals by the sum of their capacities, which keeps the number of coefficients manageable with 774 observed adjustments. The log keeps the target positive. Nothing here is structural: no cost parameter appears, and the equation is not derived from the Bellman equation (8). It is meant to approximate the equilibrium policy σ(s)\sigma(s)σ(s) well enough to simulate the industry forward.

The target is observed only when a firm adjusts, so the regression of log capacity after adjustment on the bases uses adjusters only, on the assumption that uit∗u^*_{it}uit∗​ is independent of the band errors in equation (14). The fit is very tight (adjusted R-squared of 0.9994, error variance 0.0244). Separate coefficients are estimated before and after 1990, so the investment policy may differ across regulatory regimes. Together with equation (14) it generates the investment probabilities and adjustment sizes that enter equations (17) and (22).

These two equations complete the (S,s)(S,s)(S,s) rule. Around the target sit∗s^*_{it}sit∗​ of equation (13) there is an inaction region between the lower band s‾it\underline{s}_{it}s​it​ and the upper band sˉit\bar{s}_{it}sˉit​. If current capacity sits_{it}sit​ lies inside, the firm does nothing; if it is below the lower band the firm invests up to the target, and if it is above the upper band it divests down to the target. The distance from the target to each band is the exponential of a spline index plus a normal error, so it is always positive and lognormally distributed.

The paper's equations (12) and (13) print the sum of rivals' quantities qjtq_{jt}qjt​ as the argument of the second spline. This is a misprint, and the note's equation is the corrected form. The surrounding text and the regressors of the band regression in the paper's Table VI are the sum of competitors' capacities, and a policy function must depend on the state, which consists of capacities. The argument is therefore ∑j≠isjt\sum_{j\neq i}s_{jt}∑j=i​sjt​, as in equation (13).

Estimation rests on the assumption that an observed adjustment reveals the band width, so that with symmetric bands the regression is:

ln⁡∣sit∗−si,t−1∣=λ3′ bs1(sit)+λ4′ bs2(∑j≠isjt)+uitb\ln\left|s^*_{it}-s_{i,t-1}\right|=\lambda'_3\,\text{bs}_1(s_{it})+\lambda'_4\,\text{bs}_2\left(\sum_{j\neq i}s_{jt}\right)+u^b_{it}ln∣sit∗​−si,t−1​∣=λ3′​bs1​(sit​)+λ4′​bs2​​j=i∑​sjt​​+uitb​

with uitbu^b_{it}uitb​ the common band error. The estimated error variance is 1.40 and the adjusted R-squared 0.8952.

In the forward simulation the rule yields the probability of investment. Given a target above current capacity, the firm invests when the gap exceeds the band width, and with a normal band error of standard deviation σb\sigma_bσb​:

Pr⁡(sit<s‾it)=Φ(ln⁡(sit∗−sit)−λ3′ bs1(sit)−λ4′ bs2(∑j≠isjt)σb)\Pr\left(s_{it}<\underline{s}_{it}\right)=\Phi\left(\frac{\ln(s^*_{it}-s_{it})-\lambda'_3\,\text{bs}_1(s_{it})-\lambda'_4\,\text{bs}_2\left(\sum_{j\neq i}s_{jt}\right)}{\sigma_b}\right)Pr(sit​<s​it​)=Φ​σb​ln(sit∗​−sit​)−λ3′​bs1​(sit​)−λ4′​bs2​(∑j=i​sjt​)​​

Divestment requires a target below current capacity, so given the target the two events exclude each other. These probabilities are the pi(s)p_i(s)pi​(s) and pd(s)p_d(s)pd​(s) of equation (17).

This is the first-step entry policy: the probability that the potential entrant of a market (a firm with si=0s_i=0si​=0) is active next period, χi=1\chi_i=1χi​=1, as a probit in the state. Here Φ\PhiΦ is the standard normal distribution function, ψ1\psi_1ψ1​ a constant, ψ2\psi_2ψ2​ the coefficient on the total capacity of incumbents (in thousands of tons), and ψ3\psi_3ψ3​ the shift for years after 1990. There is one potential entrant per market and year, so the sample is the 414 market-years and the dependent variable is whether an entry occurred.

The equation is a reduced form for the structural rule derived in equation (9): the entrant enters when κi+γ1i≤EVe(s)\kappa_i+\gamma_{1i}\leq EV^e(s)κi​+γ1i​≤EVe(s). Under normal draws the true entry probability is a normal distribution function of EVe(s)EV^e(s)EVe(s), equation (27), and the probit index is a linear approximation to that standardized value. The post-1990 dummy lets the whole relation shift, which is how a change in the entry cost distribution can show up in behaviour.

The preferred estimates are ψ1=−1.715\psi_1=-1.715ψ1​=−1.715, ψ2=0.0000448\psi_2=0.0000448ψ2​=0.0000448 (statistically insignificant) and ψ3=−0.609\psi_3=-0.609ψ3​=−0.609. For a market with 3 million tons of incumbent capacity the index is about −1.58-1.58−1.58 before 1990 and −2.19-2.19−2.19 after, so:

Pr⁡(entry)≈Φ(−1.58)=0.057before 1990,Φ(−2.19)=0.014after 1990\Pr(\text{entry})\approx\Phi(-1.58)=0.057\quad\text{before 1990},\qquad\Phi(-2.19)=0.014\quad\text{after 1990}Pr(entry)≈Φ(−1.58)=0.057before 1990,Φ(−2.19)=0.014after 1990

The fall reflects 15 entries before 1990 and 4 after. Since ψ2\psi_2ψ2​ is close to zero, entry probabilities vary little across states, which leaves limited variation for separating the mean from the variance of entry costs in equation (28). The fitted probabilities are the left-hand side of equation (27).

This is the first-step exit policy: the probability that an incumbent (si>0s_i>0si​>0) is not active next period, χi=0\chi_i=0χi​=0, as a probit in its own capacity sits_{it}sit​, the total capacity of its rivals and a post-1990 dummy. It is estimated on the 2233 plant-year observations.

It is the reduced form of the exit rule in the value function (8): a firm exits when its scrap value exceeds the expected value of continuing, equation (18). Own capacity and rivals' capacity matter because they determine that continuation value. The signs agree with this reading. The preferred estimates are ψ4=−1.001\psi_4=-1.001ψ4​=−1.001, ψ5=−0.00157\psi_5=-0.00157ψ5​=−0.00157, ψ6=0.0000456\psi_6=0.0000456ψ6​=0.0000456 and ψ7=−0.595\psi_7=-0.595ψ7​=−0.595, with capacities in thousands of tons: larger firms have more to lose and exit less, firms facing more rival capacity exit slightly more, and after 1990 exit is much rarer. At the sample means the paper reports that the dummy lowers the exit probability from 2.1 to 0.4 percent (51 exits before 1990, 6 after). In units of own capacity the dummy is worth:

ψ7ψ5=−0.595−0.00157≈380 thousand tons per year\frac{\psi_7}{\psi_5}=\frac{-0.595}{-0.00157}\approx380\ \text{thousand tons per year}ψ5​ψ7​​=−0.00157−0.595​≈380 thousand tons per year

(the paper's text gives 368).

The fitted probability is the pe(s)p_e(s)pe​(s) of the second step. It enters the expected payoff (17) as the weight on the scrap value, it is the argument of the spline for the conditional mean of the scrap value in equation (19), and through equation (18) it reveals the continuation value in units of the scrap value distribution. That exit falls after 1990 while the estimated scrap value distribution barely moves is the model's way of saying that incumbency became more valuable.

The first equality defines the mean of the investment fixed cost among firms that invest. By the derivation of equation (8), a continuing firm invests when investing beats both alternatives:

The left-hand side is the expected per-period payoff of equation (17), written with the action argument aaa. Substitute the spline approximations (19) and (20), and the analogue of (20) for divestment with coefficients θγ,4\theta_{\gamma,4}θγ,4​, into equation (17):

Eεiπi=  πˉi(s)⋅1−γ2 pi(s)xi−γ3 pi(s)xi2−θγ,1⋅pi(s) bs(pi(s))−γ5 pd(s)xi−γ6 pd(s)xi2−θγ,4⋅pd(s) bs(pd(s))+θϕ⋅pe(s) bs(pe(s))\begin{aligned} E_{\varepsilon_i}\pi_i=\;&\bar{\pi}_i(s)\cdot1-\gamma_2\,p_i(s)x_i-\gamma_3\,p_i(s)x_i^2-\theta_{\gamma,1}\cdot p_i(s)\,\text{bs}(p_i(s))\\ &-\gamma_5\,p_d(s)x_i-\gamma_6\,p_d(s)x_i^2-\theta_{\gamma,4}\cdot p_d(s)\,\text{bs}(p_d(s))+\theta_\phi\cdot p_e(s)\,\text{bs}(p_e(s)) \end{aligned}Eεi​​πi​=​πˉi​(s)⋅1−γ2​pi​(s)xi​−γ3​pi​(s)xi2​−θγ,1​⋅pi​(s)bs(pi​(s))−γ5​pd​(s)xi​−γ6​pd​(s)xi2​−θγ,4​⋅pd​(s)bs(pd​(s))+θϕ​⋅pe​(s)bs(pe​(s))​

Every unknown parameter multiplies a quantity that is known once the first step is done: the choice probabilities, the adjustment sizes prescribed by the policy, and spline basis functions evaluated at the probabilities. Stack the parameters and their multipliers:

θ=(γ2,  γ3,  θγ,1,  γ5,  γ6,  θγ,4,  θϕ)ζ(s)=(−pixi,  −pixi2,  −pi bs(pi),  −pdxi,  −pdxi2,  −pd bs(pd),  pe bs(pe))\begin{aligned} \theta&=\left(\gamma_2,\;\gamma_3,\;\theta_{\gamma,1},\;\gamma_5,\;\gamma_6,\;\theta_{\gamma,4},\;\theta_\phi\right)\\ \zeta(s)&=\left(-p_ix_i,\;-p_ix_i^2,\;-p_i\,\text{bs}(p_i),\;-p_dx_i,\;-p_dx_i^2,\;-p_d\,\text{bs}(p_d),\;p_e\,\text{bs}(p_e)\right) \end{aligned}θζ(s)​=(γ2​,γ3​,θγ,1​,γ5​,γ6​,θγ,4​,θϕ​)=(−pi​xi​,−pi​xi2​,−pi​bs(pi​),−pd​xi​,−pd​xi2​,−pd​bs(pd​),pe​bs(pe​))​

Then the expected payoff is the inner product in the target equation, with the product-market profit as the first element of the row vector and the known coefficient 1 as the first element of the column vector.

The paper does not list the elements of ζ\zetaζ; the vector above is what equations (17), (19) and (20) imply. Under the plus sign that the paper prints on the divestment term, the three divestment entries of ζ\zetaζ would change sign. The representation is exact given the spline approximation of the conditional means: because those means are replaced by functions linear in coefficients, even the distributions of the private draws enter linearly. Two elements matter for what follows. The coefficient 1 on πˉi\bar{\pi}_iπˉi​ fixes the scale of the payoff in dollars, which is what identifies the level of the cost parameters. And linearity carries over to discounted sums, which gives equations (22) and (23).

This defines the building block of the simulation estimator. WiW_iWi​ is a row vector with the same dimension as the row vector in equation (21): its first element is the expected discounted sum of firm iii's product-market profits, and the remaining elements are the expected discounted sums of each component of ζ\zetaζ, that is, of the expected investment volumes, squared volumes, exit events and spline terms that multiply the unknown parameters. The sum starts at the current period t′=0t'=0t′=0 and is discounted with β=0.9\beta=0.9β=0.9. The argument is written si,t+t′s_{i,t+t'}si,t+t′​, but the terms depend on the whole state vector of the market at that date.

The expectation Eσ(s)E_{\sigma(s)}Eσ(s)​ is over the future paths of the state when all firms follow the policies σ\sigmaσ: firm iii's own policy and the rivals' policies determine investment, entry and exit along each path, and after firm iii exits all its later terms are zero. Nothing in the definition depends on θ\thetaθ. The policies are the estimated first-step functions (13) to (16), the profits come from the estimated demand and cost functions, and so WiW_iWi​ can be computed before any dynamic parameter is known.

In practice it is computed by forward simulation: from a starting state, draw the investment, entry and exit outcomes implied by the policy functions, record the row vector each period, discount, sum, and average over simulated paths. The horizon can be truncated because the weights vanish geometrically:

β100=0.9100≈2.7×10−5\beta^{100}=0.9^{100}\approx2.7\times10^{-5}β100=0.9100≈2.7×10−5

Changing firm iii's policy to an alternative σ~i\tilde{\sigma}_iσ~i​ while keeping rivals at σ−i\sigma_{-i}σ−i​ gives a different vector, Wi(s;σ~i,σ−i)W_i(s;\tilde{\sigma}_i,\sigma_{-i})Wi​(s;σ~i​,σ−i​), and comparing the two is the content of equation (24).

The value of firm iii at state sts_tst​, before its private draws are known, is the expected discounted sum of its per-period payoffs when everyone follows σ\sigmaσ. This is the ex ante version EεiViE_{\varepsilon_i}V_iEεi​​Vi​ of the value function (8), unrolled forward:

Vi(st;σ(s),θ)=Eσ(s)∑t′=0∞βt′πi(st+t′,at+t′;θ)V_i(s_t;\sigma(s),\theta)=E_{\sigma(s)}\sum_{t'=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t'}\pi_i(s_{t+t'},a_{t+t'};\theta)Vi​(st​;σ(s),θ)=Eσ(s)​t′=0∑∞​βt′πi​(st+t′​,at+t′​;θ)

where by the law of iterated expectations each period's payoff can be replaced by its expectation over that period's private draws, equation (17). Substitute the linear representation (21):

Vi(st;σ(s),θ)=Eσ(s)∑t′=0∞βt′[πˉi(si,t+t′)ζ(si,t+t′)]⋅[1θ]′V_i(s_t;\sigma(s),\theta)=E_{\sigma(s)}\sum_{t'=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t'}\left[\bar{\pi}_i(s_{i,t+t'})\quad\zeta(s_{i,t+t'})\right]\cdot\left[1\quad\theta\right]'Vi​(st​;σ(s),θ)=Eσ(s)​t′=0∑∞​βt′[πˉi​(si,t+t′​)ζ(si,t+t′​)]⋅[1θ]′

The column vector is a constant: it does not depend on the date or on the path. The distribution of paths does not depend on θ\thetaθ either, because the policies σ\sigmaσ are held fixed at their first-step estimates. The column vector can therefore be taken out of the sum and of the expectation:

Vi(st;σ(s),θ)=(Eσ(s)∑t′=0∞βt′[πˉi(si,t+t′)ζ(si,t+t′)])⋅[1θ]′=Wi(st;σ(s))⋅[1θ]′V_i(s_t;\sigma(s),\theta)=\left(E_{\sigma(s)}\sum_{t'=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t'}\left[\bar{\pi}_i(s_{i,t+t'})\quad\zeta(s_{i,t+t'})\right]\right)\cdot\left[1\quad\theta\right]'=W_i(s_t;\sigma(s))\cdot\left[1\quad\theta\right]'Vi​(st​;σ(s),θ)=(Eσ(s)​t′=0∑∞​βt′[πˉi​(si,t+t′​)ζ(si,t+t′​)])⋅[1θ]′=Wi​(st​;σ(s))⋅[1θ]′

using the definition (22). The value function is linear in θ\thetaθ for given policies. This is not true of the equilibrium value function as a function of the primitives, since in equilibrium the policies change with θ\thetaθ; it holds here because the two-step method evaluates values at the observed policies. The practical gain is that WiW_iWi​ is simulated once and the value at any trial θ\thetaθ is a single inner product.

Start from the equilibrium condition (10) in its ex ante form: at the true parameters, the equilibrium policy σi∗\sigma^*_iσi∗​ gives firm iii at least the value of any alternative σ~i\tilde{\sigma}_iσ~i​ when rivals play σ−i\sigma_{-i}σ−i​. Apply equation (23) to both sides. Each policy pair generates its own distribution of paths and hence its own vector WiW_iWi​, but the same parameter vector:

Wi(s;σi∗,σ−i)⋅[1θ]′≥Wi(s;σ~i,σ−i)⋅[1θ]′W_i(s;\sigma^*_i,\sigma_{-i})\cdot\left[1\quad\theta\right]'\geq W_i(s;\tilde{\sigma}_i,\sigma_{-i})\cdot\left[1\quad\theta\right]'Wi​(s;σi∗​,σ−i​)⋅[1θ]′≥Wi​(s;σ~i​,σ−i​)⋅[1θ]′

Move everything to one side and use linearity to factor out the parameter vector:

[Wi(s;σ~i,σ−i)−Wi(s;σi∗,σ−i)]⋅[1θ]′≤0\left[W_i(s;\tilde{\sigma}_i,\sigma_{-i})-W_i(s;\sigma^*_i,\sigma_{-i})\right]\cdot\left[1\quad\theta\right]'\leq0[Wi​(s;σ~i​,σ−i​)−Wi​(s;σi∗​,σ−i​)]⋅[1θ]′≤0

The left-hand side is defined as g(σ~i;θ)g(\tilde{\sigma}_i;\theta)g(σ~i​;θ), the target equation. It is the gain in value to firm iii from switching to the alternative policy, so the equilibrium requirement is g(σ~i;θ)≤0g(\tilde{\sigma}_i;\theta)\leq0g(σ~i​;θ)≤0 for every alternative, and a positive value is a profitable deviation, a violation.

Splitting the first element of WiW_iWi​ from the rest, written WiπˉW^{\bar{\pi}}_iWiπˉ​ and WiζW^{\zeta}_iWiζ​, shows how the function depends on the parameters:

g(σ~i;θ)=[Wiπˉ(s;σ~i,σ−i)−Wiπˉ(s;σi∗,σ−i)]+[Wiζ(s;σ~i,σ−i)−Wiζ(s;σi∗,σ−i)]⋅θ′g(\tilde{\sigma}_i;\theta)=\left[W^{\bar{\pi}}_i(s;\tilde{\sigma}_i,\sigma_{-i})-W^{\bar{\pi}}_i(s;\sigma^*_i,\sigma_{-i})\right]+\left[W^{\zeta}_i(s;\tilde{\sigma}_i,\sigma_{-i})-W^{\zeta}_i(s;\sigma^*_i,\sigma_{-i})\right]\cdot\theta'g(σ~i​;θ)=[Wiπˉ​(s;σ~i​,σ−i​)−Wiπˉ​(s;σi∗​,σ−i​)]+[Wiζ​(s;σ~i​,σ−i​)−Wiζ​(s;σi∗​,σ−i​)]⋅θ′

The first bracket is the change in discounted product-market profits caused by the deviation; it is a known number. The second is the change in discounted investment volumes, exit events and spline terms, weighted by the unknown costs. A deviation toward more investment raises the first bracket and makes the investment entries of the second more negative, so it is unprofitable only if investment costs are high enough. Each alternative policy thus gives one linear inequality in θ\thetaθ, which is the input to the criterion (25).

This is the minimum-distance criterion of the second step. Each σ~i,j\tilde{\sigma}_{i,j}σ~i,j​ is one of nk=1250n_k=1250nk​=1250 alternative policies, obtained by perturbing the estimated policy functions (for example adding a standard normal error to the index of the exit probit (16)) at a starting state. For each one, ggg from equation (24) is the gain from the deviation at a trial θ\thetaθ. The indicator keeps only profitable deviations, g>0g>0g>0, which are violations of the equilibrium condition (10), and the square penalizes large violations more than small ones. Inequalities that are satisfied contribute nothing. The summand equals the square of the positive part of ggg:

1(g>0) g2=(max⁡{g,0})21(g>0)\,g^2=\left(\max\{g,0\}\right)^21(g>0)g2=(max{g,0})2

which is continuous and once differentiable in θ\thetaθ, and since ggg is linear in θ\thetaθ it is also convex.

At the true parameters with error-free first-step estimates every ggg is nonpositive and the criterion is zero; the estimator is the θ\thetaθ that brings the sample criterion closest to that. Identification comes from alternatives that pull in opposite directions: policies that invest more are unprofitable only if costs are high enough, policies that invest less only if costs are low enough, so the inequalities bracket the parameters. The scale is fixed by the product-market profit, which enters ggg with a known coefficient of one. At θ=0\theta=0θ=0 the gain reduces to the change in discounted profits, which is positive for every deviation toward larger capacity, so the criterion is not minimized there.

The paper minimizes with the Laplace-type estimator of Chernozhukov and Hong, which replaces numerical optimization by Markov chain sampling from a quasi-posterior built from the criterion and reports its mean. This is convenient because the criterion contains simulation error and can be nearly flat. Because WiW_iWi​ does not depend on θ\thetaθ, evaluating the criterion at a new θ\thetaθ requires only 1250 inner products.

This is the entrant's value function (9) rewritten for the estimation of entry costs. Start from equation (9) and abbreviate the discounted integral over next period's states as a conditional expectation of the incumbent's value:

where the right-hand side depends on xxx through the entrant's own capacity next period, although the abbreviated notation does not show it. EVe(s)=μκ+μγ++σκ2+σγ+2  Φ−1(p),E[κi+γ1i∣entry]=μκ+μγ+−σκ2+σγ+2  Φ′(Φ−1(p))pEV^e(s)=\mu_\kappa+\mu^+_\gamma+\sqrt{\sigma^2_\kappa+\sigma^{+2}_\gamma}\;\Phi^{-1}(p),\qquad E\left[\kappa_i+\gamma_{1i}\mid\text{entry}\right]=\mu_\kappa+\mu^+_\gamma-\sqrt{\sigma^2_\kappa+\sigma^{+2}_\gamma}\;\frac{\Phi'\left(\Phi^{-1}(p)\right)}{p}EVe(s)=μκ​+μγ+​+σκ2​+σγ+2​​Φ−1(p),E[κi​+γ1i​∣entry]=μκ​+μγ+​−σκ2​+σγ+2​​pΦ′(Φ−1(p))​

The investment draw is negligible in the sum: σγ+\sigma^+_\gammaσγ+​ is about 0.1 to 0.2 million dollars against σκ\sigma_\kappaσκ​ of about 100 million, and μγ+\mu^+_\gammaμγ+​ about one million against μκ\mu_\kappaμκ​ of about 200 million. With the post-1990 estimates and an entry probability of 0.014, Φ−1(p)=−2.19\Phi^{-1}(p)=-2.19Φ−1(p)=−2.19 and the implied value of entry is about 224.6−97.4×2.19≈11224.6-97.4\times2.19\approx11224.6−97.4×2.19≈11 million dollars: only draws from the far left tail of the entry cost distribution lead to entry, which is why the paper reports the probability of draws below 10 and 50 million dollars. A normal distribution also puts some mass on negative entry costs, 3.7 percent before 1990 and 1.1 percent after.

This is the nonlinear least squares problem that recovers the distribution of sunk entry costs. For each of NSNSNS states sis_isi​ (here iii indexes states, not firms) there are two numbers. One is the empirical entry probability Pr⁡(entry∣si)\Pr(\text{entry}\mid s_i)Pr(entry∣si​), the fitted value of the entry probit (15). The other is the model's entry probability from equation (27), the normal distribution function of the sum of the two fixed-cost draws evaluated at the simulated value of entry EVe(si)EV^e(s_i)EVe(si​). The parameters μκ\mu_\kappaμκ​ and σκ2\sigma^2_\kappaσκ2​ are chosen to minimize the average squared gap; μγ+\mu^+_\gammaμγ+​ and σγ+2\sigma^{+2}_\gammaσγ+2​ are held at their second-step estimates. The states are a grid of incumbent capacities from 500 thousand to 3 million tons in steps of 5 thousand, about 500 points.

Identification is transparent after applying the inverse standard normal to both probabilities. An exact fit would require:

Φ−1(Pr⁡(entry∣si))=EVe(si)−μκ−μγ+σκ2+σγ+2\Phi^{-1}\left(\Pr(\text{entry}\mid s_i)\right)=\frac{EV^e(s_i)-\mu_\kappa-\mu^+_\gamma}{\sqrt{\sigma^2_\kappa+\sigma^{+2}_\gamma}}Φ−1(Pr(entry∣si​))=σκ2​+σγ+2​​EVe(si​)−μκ​−μγ+​​

This is a straight line in EVe(si)EV^e(s_i)EVe(si​). Its slope is the reciprocal of the standard deviation of the sum and its intercept gives the mean: how fast entry probabilities rise with the value of entry across states pins down the dispersion, and the level of entry pins down the mean. Two states with different values of entry would suffice; with many states the parameters are overidentified and least squares averages. Because the probit coefficient on incumbent capacity in equation (15) is small, the left-hand side varies little across states, so the dispersion rests on limited variation.

The problem is solved separately with pre-1990 and post-1990 inputs. The results are a mean of 182.6 and 223.3 million dollars and a standard deviation of 101.9 and 97.4 million dollars. Recomputing from these normal parameters, the probability of a draw below 10 million dollars is 4.5 percent before and 1.4 percent after, and below 50 million dollars 9.7 and 3.8 percent, in line with the paper's text. The mean rises by 22 percent and the standard deviation falls by 4.4 percent (the variance by 8.6 percent); the paper's statement that the variance fell by about 4 percent refers to the standard deviation.
